transitivity: both — transitive (*clean the oven*), intransitive (*I clean on Saturdays*)
gloss: To remove dirt from something.
examples: I *clean* the bathroom every Saturday.
She *cleaned* the whole apartment in three hours.
The windows haven't been *cleaned* since spring.

transitivity: both — transitive (*wash the dishes*), intransitive (*this sweater washes well*)
gloss: To clean something with water, usually with soap.
examples: *Wash* your hands before dinner.
He *washed* the car in the driveway.
I'm *washing* the sheets today.
contrast: After *-sh* the third person takes *-es*: *washes*, never *washs*.

gloss: To wash something with clean water to get the soap or dirt off.
examples: *Rinse* the plate before you put it in the dishwasher.
She *rinsed* the lettuce twice.
I'm *rinsing* the paintbrushes in the sink.

transitivity: both — transitive (*scrub the floor*), intransitive (*you have to scrub harder*)
gloss: To rub something hard with a brush or cloth to get it clean.
examples: You have to *scrub* to get that stain out.
He *scrubbed* the pot for ten minutes.
She has been *scrubbing* the tile all morning.
contrast: One vowel + one consonant at the end, so the *b* doubles: *scrubbed*, *scrubbing*.

gloss: To wash a floor with a mop.
examples: I *mop* the kitchen twice a week.
Someone *mopped* the hallway and left it wet.
He was *mopping* the floor when the phone rang.
contrast: The *p* doubles: *mopped*, *mopping* — compare *hoped*, *hoping*, where the long vowel keeps one *p*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*vacuum the rug*), intransitive (*he vacuums on Fridays*)
gloss: To clean a floor or a rug with a vacuum cleaner.
examples: Could you *vacuum* the living room?
I already *vacuumed* upstairs.
She's *vacuuming*, so she can't hear you.
contrast: Two *u*'s in the middle: *vacuum*, not *vacum* or *vaccum*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*dust the shelves*), intransitive (*she dusts every week*)
gloss: To wipe the dust off furniture and shelves.
examples: I need to *dust* the bookshelves.
She *dusted* the whole room before the guests arrived.
He's *dusting* the picture frames.
contrast: *Dust the shelf* means take dust off, but *dust the cake with sugar* means put a fine layer on — the same verb, opposite directions.

gloss: To rub a surface until it shines.
examples: *Polish* the silver before Thanksgiving.
He *polished* his shoes on Sunday night.
The table has been *polished* to a shine.
contrast: The verb is *PAH-lish*; the nationality *Polish* is *POH-lish*, with a long *o*.

gloss: To clean or dry a surface by moving a cloth across it.
examples: *Wipe* the counter, please.
She *wiped* the table with a damp cloth.
I'm *wiping* the mirror now.

gloss: To clean a surface by rubbing it hard with something rough.
examples: You'll have to *scour* the pan to get the burned rice off.
He *scoured* the sink until it was white again.
She spent an hour *scouring* the grill.

gloss: To polish something with a soft cloth until it shines.
examples: *Buff* the wood with a dry cloth.
He *buffed* the faucet until it gleamed.
The floors had been *buffed* that morning.

gloss: To wash and iron clothes or linens.
examples: The hotel *launders* the towels every day.
She *laundered* the curtains before hanging them back up.
Freshly *laundered* sheets smell wonderful.
contrast: In the news *launder* also means to hide dirty money — *launder money* — so context decides the sense.

gloss: To make something white or lighter with a strong chemical.
examples: Don't *bleach* that shirt — it's colored.
He *bleached* the kitchen towels.
The sun had *bleached* the curtains almost white.
contrast: After *-ch* the third person takes *-es*: *bleaches*.

gloss: To clean something with a chemical that kills germs.
examples: *Disinfect* the cutting board after you use it for chicken.
The nurse *disinfected* the counter.
Every doorknob had been *disinfected* twice.

gloss: To clean something so that it is free of germs.
examples: The restaurant *sanitizes* the tables between customers.
She *sanitized* the baby bottles.
They were *sanitizing* the carts at the door.
contrast: American spelling *sanitize*; the British write *sanitise*.

gloss: To kill all the germs on something, usually with heat or chemicals.
examples: You have to *sterilize* the jars before you fill them.
He *sterilized* the tweezers in boiling water.
The bottles have all been *sterilized*.

gloss: To remove a bad smell from a place or a thing.
examples: Baking soda will *deodorize* the fridge.
She *deodorized* the carpet after the dog got sick.
They're *deodorizing* the whole basement.

gloss: To make a room or a thing smell and feel clean again.
examples: A little vinegar will *freshen* the drain.
She *freshened* the guest room with clean sheets and an open window.
Candles were *freshening* the air after dinner.

transitivity: both — transitive (*dry the dishes*), intransitive (*the towels dried fast*)
gloss: To take the water out of something, or to lose water.
examples: *Dry* your hands on the blue towel.
The laundry *dried* on the line in two hours.
The paint is still *drying*.
contrast: Consonant + *-y*: *dries*, *dried* — but the *-ing* form keeps the *y*: *drying*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*soak the pan*), intransitive (*let it soak*)
gloss: To leave something in water for a while, or to lie in water.
examples: *Soak* the pan overnight.
She *soaked* the shirt in cold water to lift the stain.
The beans have been *soaking* since morning.

transitivity: both — transitive (*lather your hands*), intransitive (*this soap lathers well*)
gloss: To rub soap into a foam, or to make foam.
examples: This shampoo doesn't *lather* much.
He *lathered* his hands and scrubbed.
The soap was *lathering* nicely under the hot water.

gloss: To wash hair or a carpet with shampoo.
examples: I *shampoo* my hair every other day.
They *shampooed* the living room carpet.
She's *shampooing* the dog in the tub.
contrast: The final *-oo* simply adds *-ed*: *shampooed*, never *shampoed*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*scrape the plate*), intransitive (*the chair scraped along the floor*)
gloss: To remove something from a surface by pulling a hard edge across it.
examples: *Scrape* the plates into the trash before you rinse them.
He *scraped* the wax off the counter with a knife.
She was *scraping* burned cheese off the pan.

gloss: To clean or smooth something with a brush.
examples: *Brush* your teeth before bed.
She *brushed* the crumbs off the tablecloth.
He's *brushing* the dog on the porch.

gloss: To pull a comb through hair to make it neat.
examples: *Comb* your hair before we leave.
She *combed* the tangles out slowly.
He was *combing* the rug for a lost earring.
contrast: The *b* is silent: *KOHM*, like *home* with a *k*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*rub the spot*), intransitive (*the shoe rubs*)
gloss: To move your hand or a cloth back and forth over a surface with pressure.
examples: Don't *rub* the stain — blot it.
He *rubbed* the spot until it disappeared.
She was *rubbing* oil into the cutting board.
contrast: The *b* doubles: *rubbed*, *rubbing*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*iron a shirt*), intransitive (*he irons while watching TV*)
gloss: To make cloth smooth with a hot iron.
examples: I hate to *iron* shirts.
She *ironed* the tablecloth before the dinner.
He was *ironing* when I called.
contrast: Said *EYE-urn*, not *EYE-ron* — the *r* is heard before the vowel, not after it.

gloss: To push down on something, or to make clothes smooth with an iron.
examples: *Press* the collar flat.
He *pressed* his suit for the interview.
The pants have already been *pressed*.
contrast: After *-ss* the third person takes *-es*: *presses*.

gloss: To bend cloth or paper over on itself so it lies neat and flat.
examples: Please *fold* the towels.
She *folded* the laundry while watching the news.
The clean shirts are already *folded*.

gloss: To stiffen cloth with starch while washing or ironing it.
examples: The cleaners *starch* his collars.
She *starched* the napkins for the wedding.
He wore a heavily *starched* white shirt.

ru: пачкать, испачкать; оставлять пятно, оставить пятно
transitivity: both — transitive (*coffee stained the rug*), intransitive (*red wine stains*)
gloss: To leave a mark on something that is hard to wash out.
examples: Be careful — beets *stain*.
The coffee *stained* the carpet.
Her apron was *stained* with grease.

gloss: To repair something torn or broken, especially clothes.
examples: Can you *mend* this tear?
She *mended* the pocket with a few stitches.
The jacket has been *mended* twice.

gloss: To cover a hole with a piece of material.
examples: I need to *patch* these jeans.
He *patched* the screen door.
She was *patching* the elbow of an old sweater.

transitivity: both — transitive (*stitch the seam*), intransitive (*she stitches by hand*)
gloss: To sew something with a needle and thread.
examples: *Stitch* the seam closed.
She *stitched* a name tag into his coat.
He's *stitching* the hem by hand.

gloss: To fold and sew the edge of cloth so it does not fray.
examples: Could you *hem* these pants?
She *hemmed* the curtains an inch shorter.
The dress still needs *hemming*.
contrast: The *m* doubles: *hemmed*, *hemming*.

gloss: To change the color of cloth or hair with a coloring liquid.
examples: She wants to *dye* the curtains blue.
He *dyed* his white socks by accident.
They're *dyeing* eggs at the kitchen table.
contrast: *Dyeing* keeps the *e*; *dying*, without it, comes from *die* and means умирать.

gloss: To let fresh air move through a room.
examples: Open a window to *ventilate* the room while you paint.
They *ventilated* the basement for two days.
The bathroom isn't well *ventilated*.

ru: убирать, убрать; наводить порядок, навести порядок
transitivity: both — transitive (*tidy your desk*), intransitive (*he tidies before guests come*)
gloss: To put things back where they belong so a place looks neat.
examples: *Tidy* your desk before you leave.
She *tidied* the kitchen in ten minutes.
He was *tidying* the garage all afternoon.
contrast: Consonant + *-y*: *tidies*, *tidied*, but *tidying* keeps the *y*.

gloss: To make something straight or neat.
examples: *Straighten* the pictures on the wall.
He *straightened* the chairs after the meeting.
She's *straightening* the shelves in the hall closet.
contrast: The *gh* is silent: *STRAY-tuhn*.

gloss: To put things in a particular order or position.
examples: *Arrange* the books by size.
She *arranged* the flowers in a tall vase.
The chairs had been *arranged* in a circle.

gloss: To put things in a different order or place.
examples: Let's *rearrange* the living room.
He *rearranged* the kitchen cabinets over the weekend.
She keeps *rearranging* the furniture.

ru: организовывать; раскладывать по местам, привести в порядок
gloss: To put things in order so you can find them.
examples: I need to *organize* the closet.
She *organized* the spice rack alphabetically.
He has been *organizing* the garage all day.
contrast: American *organize*, *organized*; the British write *organise*, *organised*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*declutter the desk*), intransitive (*we decluttered all weekend*)
gloss: To get rid of things you do not need so a space feels open again.
examples: We should *declutter* before we move.
She *decluttered* the whole basement in January.
They're *decluttering* one drawer at a time.

gloss: To take things off a surface so that nothing is left on it.
examples: *Clear* the table, please.
He *cleared* the counter before he started cooking.
The driveway has been *cleared* of snow.

gloss: To put things in a straight line with each other.
examples: *Align* the edges before you tape the box shut.
She *aligned* the shoes along the wall.
The shelves aren't *aligned*.
contrast: The *g* is silent: *uh-LYNE*.

gloss: To flatten something by running your hand over it.
examples: *Smooth* the sheet before you tuck it in.
She *smoothed* the wrinkles out of the tablecloth.
He was *smoothing* the bedspread with both hands.
contrast: The *th* is voiced, as in *this*, not as in *think*.

gloss: To make something flat.
examples: *Flatten* the boxes for recycling.
He *flattened* the cardboard with his foot.
She's *flattening* the dough with a rolling pin.

gloss: To push the loose end of cloth into a narrow space so it stays.
examples: *Tuck* the sheet under the mattress.
She *tucked* the price tags out of sight.
He was *tucking* the blanket around the edges of the crib.

gloss: To hang cloth loosely over something.
examples: *Drape* a towel over the chair to dry.
She *draped* a sheet over the couch before painting.
A blanket was *draped* across the back of the sofa.

gloss: To put something where people can see it.
examples: She likes to *display* her grandmother's plates.
They *displayed* the photos along the hallway.
The quilts are *displayed* on the wall.
contrast: Vowel + *-y*: just add the ending — *displays*, *displayed*, never *displaid*.

gloss: To put something carefully in a particular spot.
examples: *Place* the glasses upside down on the towel.
He *placed* the vase in the center of the table.
The boxes were *placed* along the far wall.

gloss: To put something in exactly the right place.
examples: *Position* the rug so the door still opens.
She *positioned* the lamp behind the chair.
He was *positioning* the shelves before he started drilling.

transitivity: both — transitive (*sort the mail*), intransitive (*we sorted for an hour*)
gloss: To separate things into groups of the same kind.
examples: *Sort* the whites from the colors.
He *sorted* the mail into three piles.
She's *sorting* the recycling.

gloss: To put something away and keep it until you need it.
examples: *Store* the winter coats in the attic.
We *stored* the extra chairs in the garage.
The blankets are *stored* under the bed.

gloss: To put things one on top of another in a neat pile.
examples: *Stack* the plates on the shelf.
He *stacked* the firewood by the door.
She was *stacking* the chairs after the meeting.

ru: сваливать в кучу, свалить; наваливать, навалить
gloss: To put a lot of things on top of each other, usually not neatly.
examples: Don't *pile* the dishes in the sink.
He *piled* the dirty laundry by the door.
Papers were *piled* on every chair.

ru: ставить на полку, поставить; раскладывать по полкам
gloss: To put things away on a shelf.
examples: The library pays students to *shelve* books.
She *shelved* the canned goods by date.
He was *shelving* the new arrivals all morning.
contrast: The noun *shelf* turns its *f* into *v*: one *shelf*, two *shelves*, and the verb is *shelve*.

gloss: To write on a container or attach a tag saying what is in it.
examples: *Label* every box before you seal it.
She *labeled* the jars with the date.
The bins are clearly *labeled*.
contrast: American English keeps one *l*: *labeled*, *labeling*; the British write *labelled*, *labelling*.

gloss: To put things into groups by type.
examples: *Categorize* the tools by size.
He *categorized* the receipts by month.
The files have been *categorized* and boxed.

gloss: To put things together because they belong to the same set.
examples: *Group* the cleaning supplies on one shelf.
She *grouped* the photos by year.
The chairs were *grouped* around the fireplace.

ru: упаковывать в коробки, упаковать; укладывать в коробку
gloss: To pack things into boxes.
examples: We need to *box* the books before Friday.
He *boxed* the china in newspaper.
Everything in the attic has been *boxed* and labeled.
contrast: After *-x* the third person takes *-es*: *boxes*.

ru: складывать в пакет, сложить; упаковывать в мешок
gloss: To put something into a bag.
examples: *Bag* the leaves and leave them at the curb.
She *bagged* the old clothes for donation.
He's *bagging* groceries at the store.
contrast: The *g* doubles: *bagged*, *bagging*.

ru: упаковывать, упаковать; складывать вещи, сложить вещи
transitivity: both — transitive (*pack the glasses*), intransitive (*she packs light*)
gloss: To put things into a box, a bag, or a suitcase.
examples: *Pack* the glasses in paper.
She *packed* the whole kitchen in two days.
He's *packing* for the trip.

transitivity: both — transitive (*unpack the boxes*), intransitive (*we unpacked all weekend*)
gloss: To take things out of a box or a suitcase and put them away.
examples: Let's *unpack* the kitchen first.
They *unpacked* every box the first week.
She's still *unpacking* after the move.

transitivity: both — transitive (*load the dishwasher*), intransitive (*the truck is loading now*)
gloss: To put things into a machine or a vehicle.
examples: Can you *load* the dishwasher?
He *loaded* the washer with towels.
The truck is already *loaded*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*unload the dryer*), intransitive (*they unloaded in the rain*)
gloss: To take things out of a machine or a vehicle.
examples: *Unload* the dryer before the clothes wrinkle.
She *unloaded* the groceries in one trip.
They were *unloading* the van in the rain.

gloss: To put something away in a safe or hidden place.
examples: *Stash* the extra batteries in that drawer.
He *stashed* the wrapping paper behind the couch.
She had *stashed* a spare key under the mat.

transitivity: both — transitive (*hoard plastic bags*), intransitive (*he hoards*)
gloss: To keep far more of something than you need instead of throwing it away.
examples: He *hoards* plastic bags.
They *hoarded* paper towels during the shortage.
She has been *hoarding* magazines for years.
contrast: *Hoard* sounds exactly like *horde* (толпа), but the spellings and meanings are different.

transitivity: both — transitive (*collect the towels*), intransitive (*dust collects on the shelf*)
gloss: To gather things together from different places.
examples: *Collect* the towels from the bathrooms.
She *collected* the cups from around the house.
Dust has *collected* on the top shelf.

transitivity: both — transitive (*gather the toys*), intransitive (*the family gathered*)
gloss: To bring things together into one place.
examples: *Gather* the dirty clothes and bring them down.
He *gathered* the toys into a basket.
She was *gathering* the leaves into a pile.

gloss: To throw something away because it is no longer wanted.
examples: *Discard* anything that's expired.
She *discarded* three bags of old paperwork.
The packaging can be *discarded*.
contrast: The verb is *dis-KAHRD*; the noun, a thing thrown away, is *DIS-kahrd*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*recycle the bottles*), intransitive (*we recycle*)
gloss: To send used paper, glass, or plastic to be made into something new.
examples: We *recycle* glass and cardboard.
He *recycled* the newspapers.
This bag is made from *recycled* plastic.

transitivity: both — transitive (*compost the peels*), intransitive (*they compost*)
gloss: To let food scraps and leaves rot so they turn into soil.
examples: We *compost* all our vegetable peels.
She *composted* the coffee grounds.
They've been *composting* since spring.

gloss: To empty something out quickly and carelessly.
examples: Don't *dump* the toys on the floor.
He *dumped* the dirty water in the yard.
She was *dumping* the ashtray into the trash.

transitivity: both — transitive (*empty the trash*), intransitive (*the room emptied fast*)
gloss: To take everything out of a container.
examples: *Empty* the trash before you go.
He *emptied* the vacuum bag outside.
She's *emptying* the dishwasher.
contrast: Consonant + *-y*: *empties*, *emptied*, but *emptying* keeps the *y*.

gloss: To take something away from where it is.
examples: This spray *removes* grease.
She *removed* the stain with cold water.
The rug has been *removed* for cleaning.

transitivity: both — transitive (*donate the couch*), intransitive (*they donate every year*)
gloss: To give something away to a charity or to someone in need.
examples: We *donate* the clothes the kids outgrow.
She *donated* four boxes of books.
They're *donating* the old couch.

gloss: To save something useful from among things that are damaged or being thrown out.
examples: See what you can *salvage* from the flooded basement.
He *salvaged* the brass handles before junking the dresser.
A few photos were *salvaged*.

gloss: To use something again instead of throwing it away.
examples: We *reuse* the jars for storage.
She *reused* the gift bags.
This container can be *reused* many times.
contrast: The verb ends in /z/ — *ree-YOOZ*; the noun *reuse* ends in /s/ — *ree-YOOSS*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*toys littered the hall*), intransitive (*please don't litter*)
gloss: To drop trash where it does not belong, or to cover a place with scattered things.
examples: Please don't *litter*.
Toys *littered* the hallway.
The floor was *littered* with wrapping paper.

gloss: To throw something away, or to leave a place wrecked and filthy.
examples: Just *trash* the broken one.
He *trashed* the old receipts.
The kitchen got *trashed* while they were making cookies.

transitivity: both — transitive (*spray the counter*), intransitive (*the hose sprayed everywhere*)
gloss: To send liquid out in fine drops.
examples: *Spray* the mirror and wipe it dry.
He *sprayed* the counter with cleaner.
She's *spraying* the windows now.
contrast: Vowel + *-y*: the *y* stays — *sprays*, *sprayed*, not *spraied*.

gloss: To scatter small drops or bits over a surface.
examples: *Sprinkle* baking soda on the carpet before you vacuum.
She *sprinkled* water on the shirt before ironing it.
He was *sprinkling* salt on the icy steps.

transitivity: both — transitive (*splash water on it*), intransitive (*water splashed on the floor*)
gloss: To make liquid fly about in drops, or to fly about in drops.
examples: Try not to *splash* when you fill the bucket.
Soapy water *splashed* onto the floor.
The kids were *splashing* in the tub.

transitivity: both — transitive (*squirt some soap*), intransitive (*the bottle squirted sideways*)
gloss: To force liquid out in a thin fast stream.
examples: *Squirt* a little soap into the sink.
He *squirted* cleaner on the stovetop.
The bottle was *squirting* sideways.

transitivity: both — transitive (*scatter the mail*), intransitive (*the crowd scattered*)
gloss: To throw or drop things so that they lie spread over an area.
examples: Don't *scatter* the mail all over the table.
The wind *scattered* the leaves across the porch.
Crumbs were *scattered* under the high chair.

gloss: To spread something soft or wet across a surface, leaving a dirty mark.
examples: Paper towels just *smear* the grease around.
He *smeared* the window trying to clean it.
The glass was *smeared* with fingerprints.

transitivity: both — transitive (*smudge the mirror*), intransitive (*wet ink smudges*)
gloss: To make a dirty or blurred mark by rubbing something.
examples: Don't *smudge* the mirror.
She *smudged* the fresh paint with her sleeve.
The chrome was *smudged* with fingerprints.

gloss: To make something dirty.
examples: Grass will *soil* white pants in a minute.
One picnic *soiled* the new tablecloth.
The *soiled* towels go straight into the hamper.
contrast: *Soiled* is the word on laundry labels and in hospitals; as a noun, *soil* means почва.

gloss: To make something slightly wet.
examples: *Dampen* the cloth before you dust.
She *dampened* the shirt and ironed it flat.
He was *dampening* the sponge under the faucet.

gloss: To make something a little wet.
examples: *Moisten* the stain, then blot it.
She *moistened* the label to peel it off.
The steam had *moistened* the whole wall.
contrast: The *t* is silent: *MOY-suhn*, like *listen* and *fasten*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*drain the bucket*), intransitive (*the sink drains slowly*)
gloss: To let liquid run out of something, or to run out.
examples: The tub *drains* slowly.
She *drained* the mop bucket into the toilet.
The dishes are *draining* by the sink.

gloss: To take in liquid so that it is no longer on the surface.
examples: These towels *absorb* a lot of water.
The rag *absorbed* most of the spill.
The paper was *absorbing* the oil.
contrast: The *s* is pronounced /z/: *ub-ZORB*, not *ub-SORB*.

gloss: To press a cloth or paper onto a wet spot so the liquid soaks in.
examples: *Blot* the spill — don't rub it.
She *blotted* the wine with a napkin.
He was *blotting* the carpet with a clean towel.
contrast: The *t* doubles: *blotted*, *blotting*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*dab the stain*), intransitive (*she dabbed at the spot*)
gloss: To touch something lightly and repeatedly with a cloth or a finger.
examples: *Dab* a little soap on the stain.
She *dabbed* at the spot with a wet cloth.
He was *dabbing* the paint off his hands.
contrast: The *b* doubles: *dabbed*, *dabbing*.

gloss: To press something tightly, often to get liquid out of it.
examples: *Squeeze* the water out of the sponge.
She *squeezed* the mop into the bucket.
He's *squeezing* the last of the soap from the bottle.

gloss: To push something briefly down into a liquid.
examples: *Dunk* the brush in the water.
He *dunked* the rag and wrung it out.
She was *dunking* the glasses in soapy water.

gloss: To put something completely under a liquid.
examples: *Immerse* the jars in boiling water for ten minutes.
She *immersed* the sponge and squeezed it out.
The base of the kettle must never be *immersed* in water.

transitivity: both — transitive (*fill the bucket*), intransitive (*the tub filled quickly*)
gloss: To put enough into a container to make it full.
examples: *Fill* the bucket with warm water.
He *filled* the sink and started washing.
The tub was *filling* while she got the towels.

gloss: To fill something again after it has been emptied.
examples: *Refill* the soap dispenser, please.
She *refilled* the spray bottle with vinegar.
The salt shaker needs *refilling*.
contrast: The verb is *ree-FIL*, stressed at the end; the noun *refill* is *REE-fil*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*restock the closet*), intransitive (*they restock on Mondays*)
gloss: To put in a new supply of something that has run out.
examples: I need to *restock* the paper towels.
He *restocked* the cleaning cabinet on Sunday.
They're *restocking* the shelves tonight.

gloss: To fill a place with a supply of things.
examples: We *stock* the guest bathroom with extra towels.
She *stocked* the pantry before the storm.
The closet is *stocked* with cleaning supplies.

gloss: To put a new thing in the place of an old one.
examples: *Replace* the vacuum bag when it's full.
He *replaced* the burned-out bulb.
The water filter has been *replaced*.
contrast: You *replace* the old thing **with** the new one: *replace the sponge with a fresh one*.

gloss: To fix something that is broken or damaged.
examples: Can you *repair* the vacuum, or should we buy a new one?
They *repaired* the washing machine last month.
The dryer is being *repaired* this week.

gloss: To repair something that does not work.
examples: Can you *fix* the leaky faucet?
He *fixed* the closet door in ten minutes.
The dishwasher still hasn't been *fixed*.
contrast: After *-x* the third person takes *-es*: *fixes*.

gloss: To keep something in good condition by taking care of it regularly.
examples: You have to *maintain* a washer or it breaks down.
They *maintained* the building themselves for years.
The floors have been beautifully *maintained*.

gloss: To put oil on something so that it moves smoothly or does not dry out.
examples: *Oil* the hinge and the squeak will stop.
He *oiled* the cutting board once a month.
She's *oiling* the wooden spoons.

gloss: To put a layer of fat or oil on something.
examples: *Grease* the pan before you pour the batter.
He *greased* the sticky drawer runners.
The garage door track had been *greased* recently.

gloss: To clear a blocked pipe or drain.
examples: Vinegar and baking soda can *unclog* a slow drain.
He *unclogged* the shower with a piece of wire.
She spent an hour *unclogging* the kitchen sink.

transitivity: both — transitive (*grease clogs the drain*), intransitive (*the filter clogs fast*)
gloss: To block a pipe or a filter so that nothing can pass through.
examples: Grease will *clog* the drain.
Hair *clogged* the shower.
The vacuum hose is *clogged* again.
contrast: The *g* doubles: *clogged*, *clogging*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*plunge the toilet*), intransitive (*he plunged for ten minutes*)
gloss: To clear a blocked toilet or drain with a plunger, or to push something down into liquid.
examples: You may have to *plunge* the toilet.
He *plunged* the drain until the water went down.
She was *plunging* the sink when I walked in.

transitivity: both — transitive (*flush the toilet*), intransitive (*the toilet won't flush*)
gloss: To send water through something to clean it out, especially a toilet.
examples: *Flush* the toilet twice if you have to.
He *flushed* the radiator hose with clean water.
The toilet won't stop *flushing*.

gloss: To close something tightly so that nothing gets in or out.
examples: *Seal* the bag so the flour stays dry.
She *sealed* the box with packing tape.
The jars are *sealed* and dated.

gloss: To rub a surface smooth with sandpaper.
examples: *Sand* the rough spot before you paint it.
He *sanded* the chair legs.
She was *sanding* the shelf all afternoon.

gloss: To take everything off a surface or a bed.
examples: *Strip* the beds and start a load of sheets.
He *stripped* the old wax off the floor.
They're *stripping* the wallpaper in the hall.
contrast: The *p* doubles: *stripped*, *stripping* — *striped*, with one *p*, means в полоску.

transitivity: both — transitive (*bathe the baby*), intransitive (*she bathes at night*)
gloss: To wash someone, or yourself, in a tub.
examples: It's easier to *bathe* the dog outside.
She *bathed* the twins one at a time.
He was *bathing* the baby when the doorbell rang.
contrast: The verb *bathe* is *BAYTH*, with a long *a* and a voiced *th*; the noun *bath* is *BATH*, short.

transitivity: both — transitive (*filter the water*), intransitive (*light filtered through the blinds*)
gloss: To pass liquid or air through something that takes the dirt out.
examples: This pitcher *filters* the tap water.
She *filtered* the used frying oil through a cloth.
The air is *filtered* before it goes back into the room.

transitivity: both — transitive (*loosen the screws*), intransitive (*the dirt loosened*)
gloss: To make something less tight.
examples: Hot water will *loosen* the stuck lid.
He *loosened* the screws on the vent cover.
The dirt had *loosened* after an hour of soaking.
contrast: The *s* is /s/, not /z/: *LOO-suhn*. Do not mix it up with *lose* (терять).

gloss: To make something firmer or closer so that it does not move.
examples: *Tighten* the faucet handle so it stops dripping.
He *tightened* the loose chair leg.
She's *tightening* the lids on the storage bins.
contrast: The *gh* is silent: *TY-tuhn*.

gloss: To take the paper or covering off something.
examples: *Unwrap* the dishes carefully.
She *unwrapped* the glasses and washed each one.
He was *unwrapping* a package of new sponges.
contrast: The *w* is silent and the *p* doubles: *unwrapped*, *unwrapping*.
